faqs.question: How long does a Torvault Fire & Burglary safe protect documents in a fire?
faqs.answer: The Fire & Burglary line carries a UL Class 350 rating: the interior stays below 350°F — the temperature paper starts to char — for a full hour, even while a surrounding fire reaches up to 1,700°F. That hour is independently tested, not an in-house estimate.

faqs.question: Is the Fire & Burglary line rated for burglary resistance, or just fire?
faqs.answer: Both. On top of its UL Class 350 fire rating, every Fire & Burglary body is forced-entry tested against common mechanical tools — prybars, hammers, punches — for a five-minute net working time on all sides. It isn't tested to the same tool list as TL-15 or TL-30, which is why Torvault treats it as the entry line rather than a high-security line.

faqs.question: What's the difference between the Fire & Burglary line and TL-15?
faqs.answer: Fire & Burglary is fire-first: a single-wall 12-gauge steel body built around a UL Class 350 fire chamber, with forced-entry resistance as a secondary feature. TL-15 is burglary-first: a 1-inch solid steel body with composite hardplate, UL-rated to resist a professional attack with power tools for 15 minutes, with fire protection available as an add-on rather than built in.

faqs.question: What size Fire & Burglary safe do I need?
faqs.answer: It depends on what you're storing and how much floor space you have. The line spans 11 sizes from the compact BF-914 up to the BF-6831 commercial vault — use the size finder and side-by-side diagram on this page to compare interior capacity and footprint against your own dimensions before requesting a quote.

faqs.question: Can I get a Fire & Burglary safe with a dial lock instead of a digital keypad?
faqs.answer: Yes. Torvault offers key lock, combination (dial) lock, and electronic keypad options across the Fire & Burglary line, so you can match your preference or any compliance requirement that specifies a mechanical lock.

faqs.question: Is a Fire & Burglary safe enough for a home office, or do I need TL-15?
faqs.answer: For home offices, retail back-rooms, and small-business petty cash or document storage, Fire & Burglary is Torvault's recommended fit — it prioritizes fire protection where forced-entry risk is limited. If you're storing higher-value inventory or need a documented forced-entry standard for insurance purposes, step up to TL-15.

faqs.question: What does the TL-15 rating actually mean?
faqs.answer: TL-15 means the door has withstood a 15-minute net working time attack by a professional safe technician using common hand tools, power drills, punches, hammers, and pressure-applying devices — the clock only runs while a tool is actively working the safe, not for the full time an attacker spends on site. It's an independent UL rating, not a self-certified marketing tier.

faqs.question: What's the difference between TL-15 and TL-30?
faqs.answer: TL-15 rates the door alone for a 15-minute net working time against hand and power tools. TL-30 doubles that to 30 minutes, adds abrasive cutting wheels and power saws to the attack tool list, and — unlike TL-15 — rates all six sides of the body, not just the door. TL-30 also steps up from a 1-inch to a 1.5-inch solid steel body.

faqs.question: Does a TL-15 safe include fire protection?
faqs.answer: Fire protection is available as an add-on rather than built into the base TL-15 specification, which is focused on forced-entry resistance. If fire protection is a requirement alongside burglary resistance, confirm the fire add-on when requesting your quote, or compare it against Torvault's Fire & Burglary line.

faqs.question: Is TL-15 sufficient for a pharmacy storing controlled substances?
faqs.answer: Yes — TL-15 is the rating most Canadian pharmacies, bank branches, and jewelry counters are built to for daytime, high-access storage. It gives you a documented forced-entry standard that insurers and regulators recognize, without the six-side TL-30 specification that cash-in-transit and high-volume operations typically require.

faqs.question: How thick is the steel body on a TL-15 safe?
faqs.answer: The TL-15 body is 1-inch solid steel, backed by a composite hardplate over the lock and boltwork, with two-way spring-loaded relocking bolts that jam the mechanism if the primary lock is attacked directly.

faqs.question: Can TL-15 safes be anchored to the floor?
faqs.answer: Yes. TL-15 units ship with pre-drilled anchoring holes for secure installation to a concrete floor, which prevents the entire safe from being removed rather than attacked in place — a common failure point insurers check for.

faqs.question: What makes TL-30 different from TL-15?
faqs.answer: TL-30 doubles the net working time to 30 minutes, adds abrasive cutting wheels and power saws to the attack tool list, and rates all six sides of the body instead of just the door. The steel body also steps up from 1 inch to 1.5 inches solid, with a 3.25-inch door and four-way relocking bolts instead of two-way.

faqs.question: Why does TL-30 rate all six sides instead of just the door?
faqs.answer: A reinforced door on an otherwise standard body only protects against an attack where the attacker chooses to go through the front. TL-30's composite hardplate and 1.5-inch solid steel extend across all six sides specifically so there's no weaker side to target — the standard cash-in-transit depots and high-volume jewelers require.

faqs.question: Does a TL-30 safe include fire protection?
faqs.answer: Yes — Torvault's TL-30 line includes 2-hour fire protection in addition to its six-side, 30-minute burglary rating, so you're not choosing between fire and forced-entry resistance.

faqs.question: Who typically needs a TL-30 safe?
faqs.answer: TL-30 is built for cash-in-transit depots, high-volume jewelers, and evidence or valuables rooms where a breach anywhere on the box — not just through the door — is an unacceptable outcome. If your risk is limited to daytime counter access, TL-15 is usually the better-value fit.

faqs.question: What does 'net working time' mean for a TL-30 rating?
faqs.answer: Net working time is the cumulative time a tool is actively cutting, drilling, or prying on the safe during UL testing — time spent repositioning, swapping tools, or pausing doesn't count. A 30-minute TL-30 rating means the safe withstood 30 real minutes of tool-on-metal attack time, independently verified by UL.

faqs.question: Can TL-30 safes be bolted down for extra security?
faqs.answer: Yes. TL-30 units ship with pre-drilled anchoring holes for secure installation to a concrete floor, preventing the whole unit from being removed and attacked somewhere else — a requirement many insurers attach to high-value coverage limits.

understanding-ul-security-ratings.title: Understanding UL Security Ratings: What TL-15 and TL-30 Actually Mean
understanding-ul-security-ratings.excerpt: TL-15 and TL-30 aren't marketing tiers — they're independently tested minutes of resistance against real tools. Here's what the numbers actually measure.
body: A "TL-15" or "TL-30" label gets thrown around a lot in the safe industry, but the number itself is the entire specification — it's a net working time, the number of minutes UL verified the door withstands a professional attack using a defined list of tools before it's considered breached.

Net working time only counts the minutes a tool is actually cutting, drilling, or prying — not the total time an attacker spends on site repositioning, swapping tools, or taking breaks. A TL-15 rating means 15 real minutes of tool-on-metal contact; TL-30 means 30. That distinction matters, because it's a much harder bar to clear than it sounds.

The rating also specifies the tool list. TL-15 testing uses common hand and power tools — drills, punches, hammers, pressure-applying devices. TL-30 adds abrasive cutting wheels and power saws to that list, which is why stepping up a tier requires a meaningfully thicker steel body, not just a thicker door.

One detail that trips people up: unless a line is explicitly rated for six sides, the UL rating applies to the door only. Torvault's Fire & Burglary and TL-15 lines rate the door; TL-30 is tested and rated across all six sides of the body, which is the standard cash-in-transit depots and high-volume jewelers typically require.

None of this is self-certified. UL is an independent third party, and it's the same standard insurers reference when setting coverage limits — which is exactly why the rating on the spec sheet matters more than the finish on the door.

fire-rated-vs-fireproof.title: Fire-Rated vs. "Fireproof": What Your Safe's Rating Really Protects
fire-rated-vs-fireproof.excerpt: No safe is truly fireproof. Here's what a UL Class 350 rating actually guarantees — and how to match it to your real fire-department response time.
body: "Fireproof" isn't a real engineering term, and no reputable manufacturer should use it without a footnote. The correct term is fire-resistant or fire-rated, and the difference isn't semantic — it describes exactly what the rating promises and what it doesn't.

A UL Class 350 rating means the interior of the safe stayed below 350°F — the temperature at which paper begins to char — for a documented period, typically one hour, while the surrounding fire reached temperatures up to 1,700°F. It's a thermal insulation guarantee for a fixed duration, not an indefinite one.

That duration is the number that actually matters when you're choosing a safe. If your building is in an area with a 10-minute average fire-department response time, a 1-hour rating gives you enormous margin. If you're protecting server backups, film, or anything with a lower char/damage threshold than paper, you need to check the specific interior temperature the manufacturer tested to, not just assume "fireproof" covers it.

It's also worth knowing that fire ratings and burglary ratings are tested completely independently. A safe with an excellent forced-entry rating says nothing about its fire performance, and vice versa — confirm both are documented if you need both, rather than assuming one implies the other.

choosing-the-right-safe-size.title: How to Choose the Right Safe Size for Your Business
choosing-the-right-safe-size.excerpt: Buying too small means outgrowing it in a year; too large wastes floor space and budget. Here's how to size a safe against what you actually need to store.
body: Sizing a safe by outside dimensions is the most common mistake we see — a model's outside footprint tells you whether it fits in your space, but it's the inside dimensions that determine whether your actual contents fit, and the two numbers can differ by several inches on every axis once you account for wall and door thickness.

Start from what you're storing, not from a size you've seen before. Measure the tallest document box, the widest ledger, the longest firearm case — whatever the largest single item is — and add a margin for the fact that a shelf, a cash tray, or a second item will usually share the space.

Then work backward from your floor. Check the per-square-foot load rating of the level the safe sits on, especially above ground floor, since a loaded TL-30 unit can weigh well over a thousand pounds. A safe that's structurally wrong for the floor it sits on is a problem no rating solves.

It's also worth sizing one tier up from your current needs rather than an exact fit, since cash, inventory, or documents tend to grow and a safe is not a purchase most businesses repeat every year. That said, there's a real cost to over-buying — a six-figure vault for a petty-cash drawer just moves the inefficiency from your shelf to your floor plan.

If you're working through this for a specific Torvault line, the size finder on each product page lets you enter what needs to fit and how much room you have, and it'll filter the lineup down to the models that actually work — and recommend the smallest one that does.

anchoring-and-installation-basics.title: Where to Install Your Safe: Anchoring, Placement, and Floor Load
anchoring-and-installation-basics.excerpt: A safe that isn't anchored can be removed and attacked somewhere else entirely. Here's what dealers check before a unit ever gets bolted down.
body: A UL rating describes how a safe resists attack while it stays in place. It says nothing about what happens if an attacker simply removes the whole unit and works on it somewhere quiet — which is why anchoring isn't an optional accessory, it's part of the security model.

Most Torvault lines ship with pre-drilled anchoring holes specifically for this reason, meant to be bolted into a concrete floor rather than wood subfloor or a mounting pad. Concrete is the baseline most insurers and dealers check for, because it resists the safe being pried free along with the anchors.

Placement matters almost as much as anchoring. A safe visible from a storefront window advertises what's behind the door; one blocked by inventory or positioned away from a rear exit removes both the temptation and the easy extraction route. Weight is a factor here too — know your floor's load rating before deciding where a safe this heavy sits, particularly on any level above grade.

Finally, think about access during installation, not just after. A safe that clears the doorway but not the hallway turn is a surprisingly common and expensive mistake — confirm clearances for the full delivery path, not just the final resting spot, before a unit ships.

why-torvault-sells-through-dealers.title: Why Torvault Sells Through Dealers Only — And Why That's Better for You
why-torvault-sells-through-dealers.excerpt: No direct-to-consumer listings, no competing with the people who install and service your safe. Here's the thinking behind Torvault's dealer-first model.
body: Torvault doesn't sell direct to consumers, and that's a deliberate choice rather than a limitation of a smaller brand. Every unit moves through an authorized Canadian dealer — the same people who will deliver, install, anchor, and service it for the life of the safe.

The alternative is common in this industry: a manufacturer sells online at retail pricing while also supplying the same dealers who are expected to compete with that listing. It undercuts the independent dealer network on price while leaving them responsible for the service relationship, which is a bad deal for everyone except the manufacturer.

Selling wholesale-only with territory protection means a dealer who takes on Torvault isn't competing against their own supplier. It also means the person selling you a Torvault safe has actually handled one, can speak to installation and anchoring specifics for your space, and has a direct line back to the manufacturer if something needs attention after the sale.

This model is backed by Security Lock & Safe Inc.'s nearly four decades running Toronto Safes — so the dealer program isn't a new idea being tested for the first time, it's the same service relationship the team has run in the GTA since 1987, extended to independent dealers across the rest of Canada.

what-to-expect-at-delivery.title: What to Expect When Your Torvault Safe Is Delivered
what-to-expect-at-delivery.excerpt: Delivery day for a several-hundred-pound safe looks different from a standard parcel drop. Here's what your dealer handles, and what to confirm before the truck arrives.
body: A Torvault safe doesn't arrive the way a parcel does. Every unit ships to your authorized dealer first, not directly to your door — the dealer coordinates delivery, confirms the final placement with you, and handles the install, so the first time you see the safe it's already positioned and ready to anchor.

Before a delivery date is scheduled, your dealer will walk through the access path with you: doorway widths, hallway turns, stairs, and elevator dimensions if applicable. This matters more than it sounds — a safe that clears the front door but not a tight hallway turn is one of the most common and expensive delivery surprises, and it's entirely avoidable by confirming clearances against the model's outside dimensions ahead of time.

Larger units — particularly TL-30 models and anything in the 1,000+ lb range — often require professional riggers or specialized equipment to move safely. Your dealer arranges this as part of the delivery, so you're not left managing equipment rental or liability on your own.

Once the safe is in its final position, installation includes anchoring it to the floor through the pre-drilled mounting holes built into the body — not an optional add-on, but part of a correctly completed install. Your dealer will confirm the floor can support the unit's weight before anchoring, especially on any level above grade.

Because Torvault sells wholesale through dealers rather than listing shipping costs online, delivery and installation pricing is quoted alongside the unit itself — ask your dealer to include it up front so there are no surprises between quote and delivery day.

fireTesting.heading: What survives a 1,700°F furnace.
fireTesting.body: Fire endurance testing is the standard methodology for record and data protection equipment. A locked safe is placed inside an industrial furnace that follows a controlled time-temperature curve reaching up to 1,700°F, while sensors continuously log the internal temperature. The safe fails the instant the interior exceeds its class threshold — anywhere inside the chamber.
fireTesting.class350Body: Interior stays below 350°F — the temperature at which paper begins to char. The standard for document and cash protection.
fireTesting.class150Body: Interior stays below 150°F — required for microfilm and other heat-sensitive media.
fireTesting.class125Body: Interior stays below 125°F — the tightest tolerance, for digital media, hard drives, and backup tape.
fireTesting.durationBodyPost: — how long the safe holds its class rating inside the furnace.

insuranceCallout.body: Most commercial property and cash-in-transit policies in Canada set coverage limits directly against a safe's UL rating — a policy might cap cash coverage at $2,500 in an unrated container versus $50,000+ behind a UL TL‑30 body. Before specifying a safe for a client, confirm the rating their insurer actually requires, not just what fits the budget.

general.q1: Is Torvault a currently certified, shipping product line?
general.a1: Torvault is a new brand launching in 2026. Specifications shown across this site reflect our engineering targets and are illustrative pending final UL certification and production — we're upfront about that rather than implying certifications we don't yet hold. Confirmed dealers receive current certification status as part of onboarding.
general.q2: How is Torvault different from Toronto Safes?
general.a2: Toronto Safes is a retail provider, selling directly to homes and businesses across the GTA since 1987. Torvault is a new manufacturing brand from the same parent company, Security Lock & Safe Inc. — built to supply independent safe dealers across Canada at wholesale, not to sell direct to consumers. See the full story on our {aboutLink}.
general.a3Pre: No safe is truly fireproof — the correct term is
general.a3Post: . A rating like “1–Hr / 350°F” means the interior stayed below 350°F for one hour inside a furnace that can reach 1,700°F outside the safe — not that the contents are immune to fire indefinitely. Match the duration rating to your realistic fire-department response time.

ratings.q1: What does a UL security rating actually mean?
ratings.a1: UL (Underwriters Laboratories) independently tests safes against real tools — prybars, drills, saws, cutting torches — for a set net working time (the clock only runs while a tool is actively working the safe). A TL‑15 safe resists a professional attack with common tools for 15 minutes; TL‑30 for 30, on every side. It's the same standard insurers use to set coverage limits. Full breakdown on our {certifiedStandardLink}.
ratings.q2: Does a higher burglary rating mean better fire protection?
ratings.a2: No — burglary ratings (Fire & Burglary, TL‑15, TL‑30) and fire ratings (measured in hours and maximum interior temperature) are tested completely independently. A high burglary rating says nothing about fire performance and vice versa. If you need both, confirm the safe carries a documented rating for each, not just one.

ordering.q1: Do you sell direct to consumers?
ordering.a1: No. Torvault sells exclusively through authorized Canadian dealers. If you're a homeowner or business looking to buy a safe directly, contact our sister company {torontoSafesLink} or ask us for a dealer referral in your region.
ordering.q2: What are the lead times for Canadian delivery?
ordering.a2: Torvault is in its first territory intake round for 2026. Confirmed dealers receive lead-time and inventory commitments as part of onboarding — request the dealer package on our {dealerProgramLink} for current timelines.
ordering.q3: How do I become an authorized Torvault dealer?
ordering.a3: Email {email} with your business name and region, or see the full application process on our {dealerProgramLink}. We'll send certified specification sheets, wholesale pricing, and territory availability.
ordering.q4: Is territory exclusive to one dealer?
ordering.a4: Territory protection is part of the dealer program — details and current availability by region are provided during onboarding, since Torvault is still in its first intake round. Reach out early to secure your area.

buildStory.ch1Body: Every Torvault body starts as solid cold-rolled steel plate — cut, formed, and welded on our production line to the thickness specified for each line, from 12-gauge RSC bodies to 1.5″ solid TL‑30 construction.
buildStory.ch2Body: Composite hardplate is bonded over the boltwork, then the relocking bolts, dial, and locking wheel are fitted and function-tested before the door is ever hung.
buildStory.ch3Title: Built to hold. Engineered to last.
buildStory.ch3Body: Every weld and every bolt is checked before a unit ships — and inspected again once it's hung, so the door opens exactly as specified.

aboutStory.ch1Title: Built on strength, driven by expertise.
aboutStory.ch1Body: With experience dating back to 1987, we deliver high-security safes for homeowners, retailers, businesses, government agencies, institutions, law enforcement, and the military — every safe built for uncompromising quality and lasting peace of mind.
aboutStory.ch2Body: Torvault was founded with a clear purpose: helping people protect what matters most. Backed by decades of industry expertise, we bring practical knowledge to a new generation of residential and commercial safes.
aboutStory.ch3Body: From personal valuables and important documents to cash, inventory, and sensitive materials — we serve homeowners, retailers, commercial and industrial businesses, government agencies, institutions, law enforcement, and military clients.
aboutStory.ch4Body: Security ratings, fire protection, lock options, and everyday access all influence the right choice. Our team helps customers understand these differences so they can make informed decisions with confidence.
aboutStory.ch5Body: From product selection and installation planning to ongoing service, we're committed to helping customers get lasting value from their purchase — earning trust through knowledgeable people and reliable protection.

manufacturingStory.ch1Title: Specified before a single unit is tooled.
manufacturingStory.ch1Body: Body, door, and locking geometry are specified against UL 72 and UL TL testing methodology before a single unit is tooled — every product line is designed to a target rating, not adapted after the fact.
manufacturingStory.ch2Body: Solid steel plate is cut, formed, and welded into the body and door blank at the thickness specified for each product line — from 12-gauge RSC bodies to 1.5″ solid TL‑30 construction.
manufacturingStory.ch3Title: Bonded over the lock and boltwork.
manufacturingStory.ch3Body: Composite hardplate is bonded over the lock and boltwork — and across all six sides on TL‑30 units — to defeat drilling and cutting attacks during UL-methodology testing.
manufacturingStory.ch4Body: Spring-loaded relocking bolts, boltwork, and the electronic or mechanical locking mechanism are fitted and function-tested before the door is hung.
manufacturingStory.ch5Body: Each product line is verified against its rated standard — fire endurance, forced-entry resistance, and lock function — before Canadian distribution begins.
manufacturingStory.ch6Title: Shipped sealed. Sold through dealers only.
manufacturingStory.ch6Body: Finished units are imported directly to Canada and shipped to authorized dealer territories — no middle-market distributor step, and no direct-to-consumer sale.
